query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a dense, nanostructured TiN barrier coating to boride-based components will significantly improve their resistance to molten aluminum corrosion during hot-dip plating.
generation.material_initial_state: As-manufactured boride-based components with typical surface finish and microstructure, without additional corrosion protection.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin (1–5 μm) TiN layer via physical vapor deposition (PVD) onto the component surface.
generation.conditions: Exposure to molten aluminum at typical hot-dip plating temperatures (approximately 660–700°C) for durations mimicking industrial processing cycles.
generation.structural_mediator: A continuous, adherent TiN coating serves as an inert diffusion barrier that prevents direct contact between the molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
generation.mechanism: The TiN layer limits interfacial reactions and inhibits the dissolution of the boride phase by restricting aluminum diffusion, thereby substantially reducing corrosion rates compared to uncoated components.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under the same hot-dip conditions, TiN-coated components will exhibit roughly a 2–3 times reduction in corrosion metrics (e.g., lower weight loss and shallower penetration depths) relative to uncoated baselines.
generation.baseline: Uncoated boride-based components exposed to equivalent molten aluminum conditions.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected to hold under standard plating temperature and duration conditions (up to about 700°C), though long-term durability under extensive thermal cycling remains to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The precise magnitude of performance improvement and the long-term adhesion of the TiN layer under repetitive thermal stress have uncertainties requiring further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set of as-manufactured, uncoated boride-based components and a second set with the applied TiN coating. Subject both sets to accelerated molten aluminum immersion tests at 660–700°C with repeated thermal cycles that simulate industrial hot-dip plating conditions.
measurements: Surface integrity and composition analysis (e.g., SEM, XPS)
Adhesion strength tests of the TiN coating after thermal cycling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the TiN-coated samples do not demonstrate at least a twofold reduction in corrosion indicators (such as weight loss or penetration depth) compared to the uncoated samples under identical test conditions, the hypothesis is falsified.
